I Drove All of the Six New Cars in Gran Turismo 7 Around the Latest Circuit in the Game
26 photos
Photo: autoevolution
My neighbor from across the road just called me to ask if I could help his son fix their new PS5. It had an annoying account connection problem, and it took me 30 minutes to find a solution. Right after, I installed “My First Gran Turismo”, which is free to play.
We then set up his Logitech steering wheel, and I gave him some pointers before returning home for a session of Gran Turismo 7. With any luck, he should be fast enough in 12 months from now so we can race together online.
I was eager to dive into part one of the new Spec IV update, as I’ve been waiting for it for several weeks now. I went straight to Collector Level 90 after the update, which is the current maximum. I’m unsure about the Concierge section right now, and I’m definitely not a fan of how the Brand Experiences kicked off.
Instead of driving some Hyundai , Polestar, Xiaomi or Yangwang, I’d like easier access to some of the top-end Porsches, McLarens and Ferraris in the game.
Anyway, I’ll be back with more info on the latest changes soon, but for now I just wanted to drive all of the six new cars at Sugo. I don’t remember ever racing this track in any other video game before, but I’ve certainly seen plenty of real world videos of it.
Citroën 2 CV 6 Charleston '86 Photo: autoevolution I guess we all knew the Citroën 2 CV 6 Charleston would be the slowest car in this new update. There’s obviously a “cure” to that problem in the form of an engine swap which I haven’t explored yet. The flat-two, 602 cc engine in this thing is only good for 28 bhp.
At least the car weighs just slightly less than three Aprilia RS660 motorcycles, which is unheard of in 2026. I figured it would be the perfect machine to learn how to deal with the 13 corners at Sugo.
It’s running on Comfort Hard tires, and I almost couldn’t believe how fast it was losing (not gaining) speed going uphill towards the finish line. I barely made it up in third gear! I then found its limit going downhill, where it could go slightly faster than “advertised” (67 mph/109 kph).
Other than being slow, it made for a pleasant drive, but I could not convince myself to go for a second lap after the first one took me just over 150 seconds to complete.
Honda Step WGN Spada Premium Line '23 Photo: autoevolution I can think of a few Honda vehicles I would loved to see before the Step WGN Spada Premium Line '23, but I’m not the one in charge of this department.
After all, the Toyota Hiace Van DX '16 needed some competition, right? The turbocharged inline-four engine in the new minivan produces 147 bhp and 149.7lb-ft of torque, with the whole package weighing more than three times as much as the Citroen.
After the first few corners it simply felt like a sportscars in comparison to the old 2 CV, but then the uphill section revealed its true colors.
It wasn’t losing speed, but barely gaining it at just over 68 mph/110 kph. It didn’t manage to hit 100 mph (161 kph) going downhill, and it was still 30 seconds faster to the finish line versus the French machine.
Honda Civic Si Group A version '87 Photo: autoevolution Two Hondas in one update must feel like a special gift for fans of the Japanese brand. I’m still a VTEC guy at heart, as I’ve never really gotten over it even after switching to rotaries.
I’ve had mixed feelings about the Honda Civic Type R (EK) Touring Car before, as it felt strange to handle at times. And I wasn’t sure what to expect of he old Civic Si Group A.
The naturally-aspirated 1.6-liter engine produces a whopping 221 bhp, with roughly four times as many kgs (or roughly nine times as many pounds) to move around. I wasn’t sure if it was much faster than I expected, or if that feeling was just a consequence of driving it after the two slower cars.
I was stunned to see the speedometer at 105 mph/170+ kph going uphill. I kept going for three laps, and the fastest one was a 1:32.986. By the time I was done, I was already in love with both the Honda and Sugo. Still, the best was yet to come.
Ferrari F355 Berlinetta '94 Photo: autoevolution Let’s face it: the Ferrari F355 Berlinetta was the most highly-anticipated car for this update. We’re getting close to 30 of them right now, and I’m hopeful we’ll get there before GT8 arrives. With 374 bhp on tap, the F355 should be capable to top out at 186 mph (300 kph).
That won’t happen at Sugo though, as the main straight just isn’t long enough. I paid 360,000 credits for this car at the Used Car Dealership, which is almost three times as much as the Honda Civic cost in the Legends Car Dealership.
As the F355 is running on CS tires, I was skeptical it could be as fast as the Civic. Let’s just say there’s plenty of “dancing” involved if you plan to keep it going straight. With that kind of oversteer “problem”, it’s considerably more fun to drive than any of the previous vehicles on this list. You can close your eyes and still recognize it’s a Ferrari judging by the exhaust and engine note.
And it sent me into a nostalgia-hole as I reminisced of simpler, more peaceful times. It might be eight seconds slower to the finish line compared to the Civic, but I’m sure some basic mods can fix that.
MAZDA RX-VISION GT3 EVO '26 Photo: autoevolution Am I the only one who’s stuck in “wishful thinking” mode after Mazda’s latest 2030 Promise video? It opens up a long list of speculations if you want to go there, including the possibility that we’ll finally have an RX-7 successor in a few years.
Seeing the RX-Vision GT3 EVO ‘26 arriving in Gran Turismo 7 further fuels that hope in my mind, especially since we already had the MAZDA RX-VISION GT3 CONCEPT and the Mazda RX-VISION '15 in the game.
At first glance, the engine setup seems identical, with chassis and aero upgrades taking center stage. The new car will cost 150,000 credits more, though.
It was a familiar, but special experience to have it out at Sugo, and I’m sure 1:24.626 is by no means an accurate reflection of its true potential. Once I get up to 100 laps at this track, I’ll try for a sub 1:20 lap.
New Time Trial Photo: autoevolution When I signed in today, the new event had only been live for a few hours. The fastest driver in the world needed roughly 77.4 seconds for a complete lap of Sugo, with the target for gold sitting at around 79.7 seconds.
Anything that’s better than 1:24.500 should be good enough for Silver, but we’ll know for sure in a few days once the dust settles. The Xiaomi deal must be a fairly good one, otherwise I can’t explain why Polyphony would have us driving the Xiaomi Vision Gran Turismo around a Japanese track.
With 2,011 bhp on tap, we’re looking at an almost 1:1 power to weight ratio here (hp to kg). That means this VGT can go up to circa 243 mph (391 kph) but also that it needs an eternity to slow down in time for the next corner.
It costs one million credits at Brand Central and I didn’t buy it yet as I’m not sure I want to. My best lap was a 1:24.275 after two attempts, and I’d rather just explore what other Japanese cars can achieve at Sugo than go again. And yes, I’ll probably be stubborn about Chinese Evs for a very long time, although I’m tempted to say “forever”. I’ll be back with a report on the new Weekly Challenges soon!
